name: Maram Naga
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Grierson, G.A. 1903. Linguistic Survey of India Vol. III Pt. II (Naga group), Maram sketch — plausibly covers pronunciation/stress; not read for a stress statement

new_statements.quote: [p. 1] The number of inventory of phonemes is twentyseven: twentyfive segmental and two supra-segmental phonemes. The segmental phonemes are (1) six vowel phonemes and (2) nineteen consonant phonemes. The supra-segmental phonemes are the two tones (1.1.2). [p. 19, §1.4.2 Tones] The two tones set up in the previous sections (1.1.2), (1.2.2) and (1.3.2) can occur both in monosyllabic or polysyllabic words. But when two vowels occur in sequence they (tones) are always marked differently - the first member is invariably falling, the second member is rising and vice-versa, except /u/ which has the same tone (see 1.4.1.2).
new_statements.citation: Pebam, Ibopishak Singh. 1984. A descriptive grammar of Maram. PhD thesis, Department of Linguistics, Manipur University, Imphal. Chapter One: Phonology, §1.0 General Remarks (p. 1) and §1.4.2 Tones (p. 19).
new_statements.locator: Ch. 1 Phonology, §1.0 p. 1 (PDF page 2 of) and §1.4.2 p. 19 (PDF page 20); tone description §1.3.2 p. 9: '/ \ / indicates a falling tone... / / / indicates a rising tone'
new_statements.rule_in_words: Maram is described as a two-tone language (falling vs. rising, contrastive on every syllable, e.g. /ammi/ 'fire' vs. 'goat', /aba/ 'debt, back' vs. 'dung, hand'); tone is the only suprasegmental phoneme recognised. The grammar never mentions word stress or accent, in the phoneme inventory, the symbols list, the syllable chapter or elsewhere, so no stress rule can be extracted; the language enters the catalog as tonal with no stress statement.
new_statements.exceptions: Only tonal: in a sequence of two vowels the tones must differ (falling+rising or rising+falling), except that /u/ keeps the same tone (§1.4.1.2, 1.4.2). Aspiration contrast noted as rare and needing further investigation (p. 1).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: tones 'can occur both in monosyllabic or polysyllabic words'; data are the spoken language of Maram Khullen village, taken by the author as the standard of all Maram dialects (Introduction). Falling and rising tones written as grave/acute over the vowel in citation forms and in the Appendix vocabulary.
new_statements.identity_note: Singh 1984 analyses the speech of Maram Khullen village, which the author takes as the standard for all Maram dialects; this corresponds to Glottolog dialect Maram Khullen Circle [mara1380] under Maram Naga [mara1379]. Author name appears as 'Pebam, Ibopishak Singh' on Shodhganga and 'Singh, Pebam Ibopishak' in Glottolog (same person). The Shodhganga thesis 'Some aspects of Maram dialect of West Khasi hills' (10603/169676) concerns a Khasi variety, not this language.

sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent anywhere: ch. 1 Phonology sets up 27 phonemes = 25 segmental + 2 suprasegmental, the suprasegmentals being two tones (falling, rising; §§1.1.2, 1.2.2, 1.3.2, 1.4.2), then syllable structure (§1.5); the Symbols page lists no stress mark; grep of the scanned text of all chapters for stress/accent/prominence/loud gives no hit. Tones occur in mono- and polysyllabic words; in vowel sequences the two tones must differ (p. 19).

sources.citation: Grierson, G. A. (ed.). 1903. Linguistic Survey of India, Vol. III Tibeto-Burman Family, Part II: Specimens of the Bodo, Naga and Kachin groups. Calcutta: Office of the Superintendent of Government Printing. 'Maram', p. 462.
sources.note: Silent. p. 462: 'I have not obtained any specimen of their language, but have inserted as many words as I could in the list of standard words and sentences. The source of these words is partly McCulloch's and partly Brown's vocabulary.... No materials are available for making even an imperfect sketch of the grammar of this language.' (The scan's earlier 'source named' is therefore a dead end for stress.)
